findings.title: initToken can throw IllegalStateException for unknown grant type, breaking token issuance
findings.body: In `initToken`, the access token ID is now built via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)` where `tokenCtx` comes from `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`. That method sets `grantType = UNKNOWN` ("na") when `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is not set on the client session context, and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` maps "na" back to "na" via the factory maps (line 78-79 of the factory put UNKNOWN->UNKNOWN), so the common path works. However, `encodeTokenId` throws `IllegalStateException("Cannot encode token with unknown grantType: ...")` when `factory.getShortcutByGrantType(...)` returns null. The factory's lazy-refresh path (`getShortcutByGrantType`, lines 106-119) only refreshes when the grant type is not found AND a provider factory exists for it; for any grant type string that is set on the client session context but has no registered `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` (e.g., a custom grant type implemented without the new SPI, or a code path that sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` to a value with no factory), `getShortcutByGrantType` returns null and `encodeTokenId` throws. Since `initToken` is on the critical path of every access-token issuance (authorization code, refresh, client credentials, CIBA, device, token exchange, etc.), any such gap turns into a 500 error at token issuance instead of degrading to the "na" shortcut. The PR sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` in several grant types but the fallback to UNKNOWN only happens when the attribute is absent — a present-but-unmapped value is fatal. Consider falling back to the UNKNOWN shortcut in `encodeTokenId` (or in `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` validating against known grants) rather than throwing.

findings.title: Removal of the Context copy constructor is a breaking API change for the SPI
findings.body: `OAuth2GrantType.Context` is a public class in `server-spi-private` and previously exposed a public copy constructor `Context(Context context)`. The PR removes it (the diff shows the copy constructor body deleted and replaced by the `grantType` initialization in the main constructor). Any third-party `OAuth2GrantType` implementation that relied on the copy constructor (a common pattern for wrapping/decorating contexts) will fail to compile against the new version. Since this is an SPI in `server-spi-private` that the PR explicitly wants to be extensible ("provider adds ability for someone to introduce his own provider"), removing a public constructor without a deprecation cycle is an API break. Either keep the copy constructor (initializing `grantType` from `context.grantType`) or document the break.

findings.title: Lightweight-token detection reads client attribute from the wrong client context
findings.body: `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` determines the token type via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, which reads `session.getContext().getClient()`. During token issuance in `TokenManager.initToken`, the session context client is the client for which the token is being issued, which is normally correct. However, for flows where the session context client differs from the client session's client (e.g., token exchange where `StandardTokenExchangeProvider.setClientToContext` sets the requesting client, or admin/service-account flows), the lightweight flag could be evaluated against the wrong client, encoding `lt` (lightweight) for a regular token or `rt` for a lightweight one. The PR's stated goal is to "recognize more reliably if access-token is lightweight or not"; deriving it from `session.getContext().getClient()` rather than from `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` undermines that reliability. Prefer `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getClient()` (the client the token is actually issued for) when deciding the token type.

findings.title: Potential NPE when client session has no user session
findings.body: `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` calls `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it (`userSession.getPersistenceState()`). For client-credentials grants and service accounts, Keycloak can create client sessions without a user session (transient service-account sessions may have a user session, but some code paths create client sessions with a null user session). If `getUserSession()` returns null, this throws a NullPointerException inside `initToken`, failing token issuance. The method should handle a null user session (e.g., treat as TRANSIENT, which matches how service-account/client-credentials tokens behave) instead of dereferencing blindly.

Worth verifying with an integration test for the pre-authorized-code flow.

findings.title: Refresh grant type is hardcoded to REFRESH_TOKEN constant instead of the actual grant type used
findings.body: In the refresh-token path (`refreshAccessToken` / the code around line 248), the PR sets `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN)`. `OAuth2Constants.REFRESH_TOKEN` is the string "refresh_token", which matches `RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.getId()`, so the encoding will produce the `rt` shortcut — but note this collides conceptually with the token-type shortcut `rt` (regular token) used in the token-type position; they are in different positions so encoding is unambiguous, but it is confusing. findings.title: Unit test bypasses factory.postInit and hand-builds maps, missing coverage of duplicate-shortcut validation
findings.body: The test's `@Before` constructs `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory`, calls `init(null)`, and then directly assigns `factory.grantsByShortcuts` / `factory.grantsToShortcuts` (package-private fields) instead of calling `postInit(...)`.
